title: India Wants Diaspora Athletes to Play for the National Team. The 'Sports Passport' Is Now on Modi's Desk.
excerpt: The Sports Ministry has sent a proposal to the PM's Office and the Home Ministry that would let PIO and OCI athletes represent India without full citizenship — a move that could reshape the country's Olympic and FIFA ambitions.
body:
The Indian government is considering one of the most consequential policy changes in the country's sporting history. The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports has sent a formal proposal to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's office and the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking approval for a 'Sports Passport' — a framework that would allow Persons of Indian Origin and Overseas Citizens of India to represent India in international competitions without acquiring full Indian citizenship.

The timing is not accidental. The FIFA World Cup 2026 is underway in the United States, Canada, and Mexico, and the question of whether India will ever qualify for one has become a recurring national lament. Meanwhile, the country is actively bidding for the 2036 Olympics. Both ambitions run into the same wall: a shallow talent pool, constrained by a citizenship requirement that excludes millions of athletes of Indian heritage scattered across the world.

What the Proposal Would Change

Under current Indian law, dual citizenship is not recognised. Any athlete who wants to represent India must surrender their foreign passport and acquire an Indian one — a process that is expensive, time-consuming, and often impractical for athletes at the peak of their careers. The most recent example is footballer Ryan Williams, who gave up his Australian citizenship to play for India.

The Sports Passport would create a parallel eligibility pathway. PIO and OCI cardholders — many of whom were born abroad but carry Indian heritage — would be able to represent the country in international events through a special framework, without the full citizenship conversion.

""Bharat Innovates is creating opportunities for Indian startups to engage with global investors," Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan said this week about a parallel initiative in Nice."

The proposal draws from models already used by Qatar, Bahrain, Turkey, Spain, Hungary, and Austria, all of which have fast-track pathways to strengthen their national teams. India would be adapting the concept to its own legal architecture.

The Football Catalyst

The immediate trigger is football. India's men's team has slipped in the FIFA rankings, repeatedly faltered in Asian competitions, and watched helplessly as athletes of Indian origin — Sarpreet Singh (New Zealand), Samuel Moutoussamy (DR Congo), Tahsin Jamshid (Qatar) — represent other countries instead.

But the implications stretch far beyond the pitch. India has historically underperformed in basketball, tennis, athletics, and swimming — disciplines where diaspora athletes, trained in world-class systems in Europe, North America, and Australia, could immediately deepen the talent pool.

"Bharat Innovates is creating opportunities for Indian startups to engage with global investors," Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan said this week about a parallel initiative in Nice. The Sports Passport applies the same logic to sport: India's diaspora is an untapped competitive advantage.

The BCCI Counterpoint

Not everyone is moving in the same direction. The Board of Control for Cricket in India recently tightened its own eligibility rules, requiring all players in BCCI-run domestic tournaments to hold valid Indian passports. The earlier policy had allowed PIO and OCI cardholders to participate.

The contrast underscores the tension at the heart of this debate. Cricket, flush with money and domestic talent, can afford to restrict eligibility. Sports where India struggles internationally — football, basketball, athletics — cannot.

What Happens Next

Sources familiar with the process say the government could take six to eight months to arrive at a decision. The proposal must clear both the PMO and the Home Ministry, and any final framework will need to navigate India's citizenship laws, international federation rules, and the political sensitivities of allowing foreign-passport holders to wear the national jersey.

For the estimated 32 million members of the Indian diaspora, the Sports Passport represents something larger than sport. It is a signal — still tentative, still unsigned — that India is willing to rethink who belongs to its national project.

The World Cup is on television. India is not in it. This proposal is one answer to why.
